name: netstat
desc: Display active network connections, listening ports and routing tables.
scenarios: Service not starting — check if the port is already bound
Find which process owns port 80 or 443
Audit all listening services before a security review

mistakes.x: Using netstat without -n causes slow DNS lookups
mistakes.fix: Always use -n to skip reverse DNS

mistakes.x: Forgetting -p hides PID info
mistakes.fix: Run as root or with sudo to see all PIDs

secnote: Attackers run netstat to map open ports. As defender: unknown listeners on unusual ports are red flags. Modern replacement: ss -tulnp (faster, more detail).
tags: port connection socket listening tcp udp pid network

name: ss
desc: Modern replacement for netstat. Faster, richer socket statistics directly from kernel.
scenarios: Preferred tool for live incident response — faster than netstat
Check if a service port is bound before starting a daemon
During IR: enumerate all outbound connections quickly

mistakes.x: Using netstat when ss is available
mistakes.fix: ss reads kernel structs directly, netstat is deprecated on many distros

mistakes.x: Not filtering output on busy servers
mistakes.fix: Pipe through grep or use destination filter flags

secnote: During incident response, ss is the first tool to run. Pay attention to ESTABLISHED connections to unusual IPs and LISTEN on unexpected ports.
tags: socket statistics network port tcp udp connection kernel

name: ping
desc: Test reachability and measure round-trip latency via ICMP echo requests.

usage.cmt: test with larger packet size (MTU check)

scenarios: First step in any network debug flow
Checking if packet loss exists before blaming the application
Testing MTU issues causing fragmentation

mistakes.x: Concluding host is down because ping fails
mistakes.fix: Many hosts block ICMP — use traceroute or nmap to confirm

mistakes.x: Not specifying -c — runs forever
mistakes.fix: Always use -c N in scripts

tags: connectivity reachability icmp latency packet loss network

name: traceroute
desc: Trace the route packets take to a destination, showing each hop and latency.

usage.cmt: TCP trace on port 443 (bypass ICMP blocks)

scenarios: Pinpointing where in the network a connection fails
Identifying a slow hop causing latency spikes
Testing if a specific port is reachable through firewalls

mistakes.x: Giving up at * * * hops
mistakes.fix: Some routers drop ICMP; try -T (TCP) or mtr for continuous trace

mistakes.x: Not using -n on slow networks
mistakes.fix: DNS lookups on each hop cause major slowdown

tags: routing hops latency path network trace hop

name: curl
desc: Transfer data from URLs. Essential for testing HTTP endpoints, APIs, and connectivity.

usage.cmt: verbose — shows full TLS handshake and headers
HEAD request — headers only, no body
check status code and response time

scenarios: Testing if an API endpoint is reachable from a server
Checking TLS certificate validity and chain
Debugging slow response times on a web service

mistakes.x: Using curl without -L misses redirects
mistakes.fix: Add -L to follow HTTP 301/302 redirects

mistakes.x: Ignoring TLS errors with -k in production
mistakes.fix: -k is for debugging only — never skip cert validation in scripts

secnote: curl can exfiltrate data or download malware. If you see unexpected curl processes, inspect the command line immediately with ps aux.
tags: http https api endpoint url request response header status code

name: ps
desc: Snapshot of currently running processes. Outputs to stdout — ideal for scripting and piping.

usage.cmt: all processes, BSD-style — shows USER PID %CPU %MEM

scenarios: Finding which process is consuming all CPU before killing it
Identifying zombie processes left by a crashed parent
Scripting process health checks

mistakes.x: Using ps alone without flags — shows only current user
mistakes.fix: Use ps aux to see all processes from all users

mistakes.x: Grepping for process name catches the grep itself
mistakes.fix: Use grep [n]ginx or pgrep nginx instead

tags: process pid cpu memory running status list snapshot

name: top / htop
desc: Real-time interactive process monitor. htop is the color-coded, mouse-friendly version.
scenarios: Investigating a server slowdown in real time
Monitoring a specific service during load testing
Capturing a one-time snapshot for a report

mistakes.x: Killing processes from top/htop without checking dependencies
mistakes.fix: Check ps --ppid PID first to see child processes

mistakes.x: Trusting a single CPU% reading — it fluctuates
mistakes.fix: Watch for 10+ seconds before concluding high CPU

tags: cpu memory load monitor processes real-time interactive

name: kill / killall
desc: Send signals to processes. kill uses PID, killall uses process name.

usage.cmt: kill by full command string match

scenarios: Gracefully restarting a hung service
Force-killing a process that ignores SIGTERM
Reloading a service config without full restart

mistakes.x: Jumping straight to -9 (SIGKILL)
mistakes.fix: Always try -15 (SIGTERM) first — gives process time to clean up and close files properly

mistakes.x: killall matching too broadly
mistakes.fix: Test with pgrep -l processname first to preview which processes match

secnote: Malware may respawn after kill if it has a watchdog process. Verify with ps after killing. If it respawns, find and kill the parent first.
tags: kill signal process stop terminate restart sigterm sigkill

name: df
desc: Report disk space usage of filesystems. First stop for "disk full" investigation.

usage.cmt: check inode usage — can be full even if disk space available

scenarios: Server stopped writing logs — check if /var or /var/log partition is full
Database crashes — often caused by 100% disk on data partition
CI/CD pipeline failing — tmp or build partition exhausted

mistakes.x: Only checking disk % and missing full inodes
mistakes.fix: Run df -i too — inode exhaustion causes "no space" even with free disk

mistakes.x: Checking the wrong partition
mistakes.fix: Always check the specific path: df -h /var/log, not just df -h

tags: disk space storage filesystem full partition usage inode

name: du
desc: Estimate file and directory space usage. Find what is consuming the disk.
scenarios: Finding which directory consumed the suddenly full disk
Identifying log bloat or core dump accumulation
Pre-migration disk audit

mistakes.x: Running du / without 2>/dev/null — floods output with permission errors
mistakes.fix: Always append 2>/dev/null to suppress permission denied messages

mistakes.x: Forgetting sort -h for human sizes
mistakes.fix: sort -rh correctly sorts 1G above 500M; plain sort -r does not

tags: disk usage space files directory size find large storage

name: chmod
desc: Change file and directory permissions. Controls read, write, execute access.

usage.cmt: rw-r--r-- : owner rw, group r, others r
rwxr-xr-x : owner rwx, others rx (standard for executables)
recursive: owner rwx, group rx, others none
symbolic: add exec for user, remove write for group

scenarios: Script won't execute — needs +x permission
Web server can't read config — wrong group permissions
Securing sensitive files to owner-only access

mistakes.x: Using chmod 777 as a quick fix
mistakes.fix: 777 gives everyone full access — use 755 for directories, 644 for files, diagnose the real issue

mistakes.x: Forgetting -R applies recursively including files
mistakes.fix: Directories need execute to be entered; files generally should not have execute unless intentional

secnote: chmod 777 is a critical security misconfiguration. If you see world-writable sensitive files, treat it as a finding. Check who modified it: stat file and check mtime.
tags: permission file access read write execute mode octal

name: chown
desc: Change file ownership — user and group.

usage.cmt: cron files should be owned by root

scenarios: Web server 403 errors because files are owned by wrong user
Deployment script creates files owned by root instead of service user
After restore from backup, ownership is wrong

mistakes.x: Chowning /etc or /usr recursively to fix one broken file
mistakes.fix: Always be specific — chown -R on system directories is destructive

mistakes.x: Forgetting the group in chown user file
mistakes.fix: Use chown user:group to explicitly set both

secnote: SUID/SGID bits combined with wrong ownership can be privilege escalation vectors. Check with: find / -perm /4000 -user root
tags: ownership user group file permission chown root

name: journalctl
desc: Query and display the systemd journal. The primary log tool on modern Linux.

usage.cmt: last 50 error-level entries across all services
kernel messages from the past hour

scenarios: Service crashed — check exact error before last exit
Investigating a specific time window after an incident
Monitoring a service in real time during testing

mistakes.x: journalctl -u service without --since dumps everything
mistakes.fix: Always scope with --since today or --since -1h to keep output manageable

mistakes.x: Missing -f for live watching
mistakes.fix: Use journalctl -u service -f to tail — much cleaner than watching the whole system log

tags: log journal systemd service error debug monitoring tail

name: grep
desc: Search text using patterns. Fundamental for filtering logs and files.

usage.cmt: show 3 lines before and after each match

scenarios: Finding failed SSH attempts in auth log
Searching application logs for a specific error across a date range
Identifying which config file contains a specific setting

mistakes.x: Not using -i for log searches
mistakes.fix: Log levels are often mixed case — -i catches ERROR, Error, error

mistakes.x: Grepping huge logs without restricting time range first
mistakes.fix: Pre-filter with awk or sed for the time window before grepping

tags: search text pattern log file filter find string

name: systemctl
desc: Control the systemd system and service manager. Start, stop, enable, inspect services.

usage.cmt: enable at boot AND start immediately
required after editing service unit files

scenarios: Service not running after reboot — check if it's enabled
Service started but immediately crashes — check status for exit code
After editing /etc/systemd/system/*.service — reload before restart

mistakes.x: Restarting without daemon-reload after editing unit files
mistakes.fix: Always run systemctl daemon-reload after modifying .service files

mistakes.x: Confusing start (now) with enable (at boot)
mistakes.fix: Use enable --now to do both at once — common to miss one or the other

tags: service start stop restart enable disable systemd unit boot

name: crontab
desc: Schedule recurring tasks. crontab -e edits user crons, /etc/cron.d/ for system-wide.
scenarios: Scheduled backup never ran — check cron syntax and log
Investigating scheduled tasks after suspicious activity
Setting up automated log rotation or cleanup

mistakes.x: Forgetting % in cron date strings must be escaped as \%
mistakes.fix: In crontab, literal % is a newline — always escape: \%

mistakes.x: New cron job not running — missing newline at end of file
mistakes.fix: crontab files must end with a newline; some editors don't add one automatically

secnote: Cron is a common persistence mechanism for malware. During IR, check ALL cron locations: /var/spool/cron/, /etc/cron.d/, /etc/crontab, /etc/cron.hourly daily weekly monthly.
tags: schedule task cron job timer recurring automation

name: useradd / usermod
desc: Create and modify user accounts on the system.

usage.cmt: -m creates home, -G adds to sudo group
add existing user to group without removing others
expire password — force change at next login

scenarios: Onboarding a new sysadmin — create account with correct groups
User locked out — check if account is locked with passwd -S
Post-incident — immediately lock a compromised account

mistakes.x: usermod -G group removes all OTHER groups
mistakes.fix: Always use -aG (append) not -G alone when adding to a group

mistakes.x: Deleting users without -r leaves orphaned home directories
mistakes.fix: Use userdel -r or manually clean /home/username after

secnote: After any suspected compromise, immediately: usermod -L username. Then audit what they accessed with: last username and ausearch -ua UID.
tags: user account create modify group sudo password lock delete

name: last / lastb
desc: Show last logged-in users. lastb shows failed login attempts.

usage.cmt: full timestamps for a specific user
who is currently logged in right now

scenarios: Investigating unauthorized access — check login history
Checking if a user was logged in during an incident window
Auditing root login activity

mistakes.x: Trusting last alone — logs can be tampered with
mistakes.fix: Cross-reference with journalctl auth logs and /var/log/secure or /var/log/auth.log

mistakes.x: Not checking lastb for brute force
mistakes.fix: Run lastb | head -30 regularly — high failure counts indicate active brute force

secnote: lastb is critical for detecting brute force. Hundreds of failures from one IP = active attack. Block with: ufw deny from IP or add to /etc/hosts.deny.
tags: login user history authentication last failed brute force

name: find
desc: Search for files by name, type, date, permissions, ownership, and size.

usage.cmt: find SUID root files — privilege escalation audit
files created since boot in temp dirs

scenarios: Disk filling up from old log files — find and purge safely
Security audit — find unexpected SUID binaries
IR — find files created or modified in a suspect time window

mistakes.x: find / without 2>/dev/null floods with permission errors
mistakes.fix: Always add 2>/dev/null to suppress permission denied noise

mistakes.x: Using -delete on find results without testing first
mistakes.fix: Run without -delete first to preview; add -delete only when result looks correct

secnote: SUID files are prime privilege escalation vectors. Any unexpected SUID binary (not in standard distro package) is a critical finding. Baseline with: dpkg -S /path/to/binary.
tags: find search file directory permission suid mtime size type locate

name: iptables / ufw
desc: Manage kernel netfilter firewall rules. ufw is the simplified frontend.

usage.cmt: list all iptables rules with packet counts
immediately block an IP (insert at top)

scenarios: Blocking an IP conducting a brute force attack
Opening a port for a new service without disabling the firewall
Auditing current firewall rules after an incident

mistakes.x: iptables -F flushes ALL rules — can lock you out of SSH
mistakes.fix: Before flushing, add an ACCEPT rule for your IP or port 22, or use ufw which is safer

mistakes.x: ufw changes not persistent if ufw is disabled
mistakes.fix: Always check ufw status is active; run ufw enable to persist rules

secnote: In an active incident, the fastest block is: iptables -I INPUT 1 -s ATTACKER_IP -j DROP. This takes effect immediately without restarting anything.
tags: firewall rule block allow port ip iptables ufw network security

name: tcpdump
desc: Capture and analyze network packets at the interface level.

usage.cmt: capture HTTP on eth0, no DNS resolution
all interfaces, traffic to/from specific host
write to file for Wireshark analysis
capture SYN packets only — detect scan

scenarios: Debugging an application that claims it's sending packets but server isn't receiving
Capturing traffic for Wireshark analysis during a network issue
Detecting a port scan or suspicious connection attempts in real time

mistakes.x: Running tcpdump without -n causes DNS lookups per packet — very slow
mistakes.fix: Always use -n to disable reverse DNS resolution

mistakes.x: Capturing on the wrong interface
mistakes.fix: Use tcpdump -D to list all interfaces; use -i any to capture all

secnote: tcpdump can capture credentials in plaintext on unencrypted protocols (FTP, Telnet, HTTP). This is exactly what attackers on your network do. Use it defensively — and ensure your network uses TLS.
tags: packet capture network traffic analysis pcap wireshark tcp udp interface
